newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi Kurds bristle at prospect of Turk incursion.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi Kurds bristle at prospect of Turk incursion.

text.p: Iraqi Kurds bristled on Sunday at the prospect of a new Turkish incursion into northern Iraq, fearing Kurds would pay a price in lives and property for an illegal border crossing whose aim remained unclear.

"We are not pleased about this rumoured move across our border by the Turks. We certainly didn't invite them and we don't know what they're up to," said Mohammad Musa, a Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) official in the border town of Zakho.
"In my opinion we are disgraced by this Turkish plan. I speak as a local official because I know of no statement from our party headquarters," he told Reuters on Sunday.

Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller has vowed Turkey will create a shallow security zone inside northern Iraq to help fight Turkish Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels who use the mountains there as a sanctuary for attacks against her country.

The Iraqi Kurds said on Sunday there still had been no confirmed citing of Turkish forces inside northern Iraq despite what were described as "massive" troop buildups on the Turkish side of the border.

Fearing a replay of past Turkish army incursions, many Iraqi Kurds in remote border villages that would fall inside a 10-km (six-mile) -deep security zone fled over the weekend rather than risk being mistaken for PKK soldiers or sympathisers.

In March 1995, 35,000 Turkish troops backed by armour and air power pushed 40 km (25 miles) into Iraq in pursuit of the separatists. The PKK, however, returned as soon as the Turks left, six weeks later.

On Sunday there were no signs of Turkish troops at KDP checkpoints. But acting on rumours of an imminent action, residents fled, some on foot and others in pickup trucks loaded with bedding, produce and firewood.
PKK guerrillas inside northern Iraq were defiant, pledging to kill as many Turks as possible before slipping away into the mountains to fight again.

"If we were frightened of the Turks we wouldn't have joined the PKK in the first place and we wouldn't be waiting for them here in the mountains," said Osman, a sentry manning a PKK checkpoint near the Turkish border.

"Every announcement they make about wiping out the PKK by crossing the border makes them look foolish. They have come many times before and we are still alive. There is no victory for them here, only death," he said on Saturday.
Iraqi Kurds were sceptical about the real purpose of the Turkish operation, also discounting the notion that it would deal the PKK a mortal blow.
"On the surface they claim their plan is aimed at the PKK. But we don't know what the deeper motive may be," said the KDP's Mohammad Musa.
Baghdad is unable to exert its authority over northern Iraq because of the Western-enforced safe haven and no-fly zone created to protect Iraqi Kurds here after the Gulf War.

A power vacuum has developed now that Iraqi Kurdish efforts at self-government have collapsed in bitter fighting between KDP forces and troops loyal to Jalal Talabani and his Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
KDP chief Massoud Barzani invited the Iraqi army to help him capture the city of Arbil a week ago from PUK forces receiving passive support from neighbouring Iran.

"Iran, Iraq and Turkey are exploiting this fighting among the Kurds but we don't want them to interfere," said Dostvan, a PKK divisional commander in the Haftenin region of northern Iraq, on Saturday.
"The Turks make this fighting their excuse to come across the border but we will fight against this trespass."
